title: Delta Air Lines 9570
summary: Delta Air Lines Flight 9570, a DC-9-14 training flight with four occupants including an FAA inspector, was on approach to Greater Southwest International Airport (GSW) at Fort Worth, Texas. The aircraft was sequenced behind an American Airlines DC-10 which had recently completed a touch-and-go landing on Runway 13. On final approach with 53-54 seconds separation from the DC-10, the DC-9 encountered severe wake turbulence from the heavy jet, causing the aircraft to oscillate about the roll axis, then roll rapidly to the right. The right wingtip struck the runway and the aircraft continued to roll until the fuselage struck in a nearly inverted attitude. The aircraft was destroyed by impact and fire, killing all four occupants.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the accident was an encounter with a trailing vortex generated by a preceding heavy jet which resulted in an involuntary loss of control of the airplane during the final approach. Although cautioned to expect turbulence the crew did not have sufficient information to evaluate accurately the hazard or the possible location of the vortex. Existing FAA procedures for controlling VFR flight did not provide the same protection from a vortex encounter as was provided to flights being given radar vectors in either IFR or VFR conditions.

factors.evidence: DC-9 encountered trailing vortex generated by preceding DC-10 heavy jet aircraft. Flight data recorders confirmed DC-9 traversed same track as DC-10 during final approach phase with only 53-54 seconds separation (p. 6)

ATC issued advisory to expect caution turbulence but did not explicitly advise crew they were following a heavy aircraft. ATC noted DC-10 in traffic but terminology heavy jet not used on radio. Separation between DC-9 and DC-10 was established at radar greater than 6 nautical miles but deteriorated on final approach due to VFR positioning (p. 5, 18)

Most prior wake turbulence accidents involved smaller aircraft than DC-9, suggesting crews had not been trained to recognize wake turbulence hazard to larger twin-engine aircraft from heavy jets (p. 25)

events.text: Delta Flight DL9570 departed Love Field, Dallas, Texas on training flight with takeoff gross weight 77,300 pounds and center of gravity 25.7 percent MAC. Aircraft carried Captain George G. Gray (check airman), First Officer, FAA air carrier inspector, and flight engineer.

Flight requested and received clearance for ILS approach to Runway 13 at Greater Southwest International Airport. Advised that American Airlines DC-10 was in traffic pattern conducting touch-and-go landings. DC-9 received advisory to expect caution turbulence.

First ILS approach completed with full-stop landing. Aircraft subsequently performed training maneuvers and was issued takeoff and climb-out clearances to maintain VFR. Gross weight approximately 74,000 pounds at time of accident (vs 77,300 at takeoff).

Flight requested and received radar vectors for second ILS approach to Runway 13, again sequenced behind DC-10 with separation exceeding 6 nm radar. Crew visually assessed traffic and became concerned about DC-10 landing conflict with planned circling approach to Runway 17.

Second ILS approach terminated with missed approach. Radar vectors provided for VOR approach to Runway 35 with circling approach to Runway 17. Tower controller subsequently cleared flight for circling approach to Runway 17.

Flight requested and received clearance for full-stop landing on Runway 13 behind DC-10 on final approach. Local controller issued clearance with advisory: Okay that'll be fine use one three for full stop! Caution turbulence. Aircraft at reference speed 130 knots, approach flown manually and smoothly with little azimuth/glide slope deviation, airspeed not varying more than 2-3 knots from approach speed of 135 knots.

DC-9 on final approach to Runway 13, approximately 53-54 seconds behind DC-10 which had completed touch-and-go landing. Aircraft flight data recorders show DC-9 traversed same track as DC-10. FDR data indicated aircraft was flying normal approach profile. Separation deteriorated from initial radar spacing due to VFR circling procedure and delayed turn to final.

Approximately 11 seconds before impact at 670 feet altitude (approximately 100 feet above airport elevation), aircraft encountered trailing vortex. Right seat occupant (Delta check pilot) commented A little turbulence here. Flight data recorder disclosed corresponding vertical acceleration trace excursion to +1.7 g. Aircraft began to oscillate about roll axis. After two oscillations, aircraft rolled rapidly to the right.

After achieving approximately 90 degrees of roll, right wingtip contacted runway surface at approximately 1,240 feet beyond runway threshold. Aircraft continued rolling to right in nearly inverted attitude. Fuselage and empennage separated upon impact and slid approximately 2,400 feet coming to rest off right side of runway. Aircraft was destroyed by impact forces and general fire which developed subsequent to impact. All four occupants sustained fatal injuries: three from massive injuries and one from smoke and carbon monoxide inhalation. CVR data disclosed stall warning system was actuated just prior to impact, indicating go-around attempt was initiated too late to prevent accident.

recommendations.text: Reevaluate wake turbulence separation criteria for aircraft operating behind heavy jet aircraft

Issue alert notices to all pilots and aircraft operators that will stress the urgent need to maintain adequate separation from heavy jet aircraft, with special emphasis on nonradar VFR procedures and need to provide time/distance separation

Develop new standards requiring 5 miles spacing for all aircraft, with exception of 747 or CSA operating behind DC-10 and L-1011 (previously required only 3 miles spacing for wide-bodied jets behind heavy jets)
Establish specific separation standards for VFR operations
Develop and implement safe spacing system where tower controller determines hazard existence
Develop automatic safe spacing using aircraft transponder signals and mini-computer to determine hazard existence and provide warning
Conduct comprehensive review of all FAA procedures and training related to wake turbulence avoidance
Establish specific training requirements for all pilots and air traffic controllers regarding wake turbulence hazards
